motifs.text: Hyphenated coinages such as 'star-glistring', 'Hee-Shee-Coupled-One' and 'Tinder-box of WAR' come partly from Du Bartas's French and partly from Sylvester's own delight in the device, and they became a fashion in English verse.

symbols.title: The book
symbols.text: The world as a book written by God, read beside Scripture: the governing image of the First Week.

symbols.title: The painter's picture
symbols.text: God contemplating his finished work like a painter admiring a landscape (Seventh Day): creation as art and the poem as a copy of it.

symbols.title: The lute
symbols.text: The harmony of creation, tuned before the Fall and untuned by Adam's sin; music also appears as Jubal's invention, David's harp and the fourth of the mathematical arts.

symbols.title: The Phoenix
symbols.text: Dying and reborn from its own ashes, an emblem of death in Adam and life in Christ.

symbols.title: Babel
symbols.text: The tower of human pride and the origin of the diversity of languages, which makes all present speech a 'counterfeit' coin.

debates.title: Protestant poetics and the sacred epic
text: Barbara Lewalski's account of a Protestant poetics in seventeenth-century England, grounded in the Bible's own genres and in a habit of applying Scripture to the self, gave Du Bartas a central place among the models for English religious verse. His programme of turning poetry from love to God, and his figure of Urania as the Christian Muse, were taken up by English writers from the 1580s onwards, as Lily Campbell showed in her study of 'divine poetry' [[lewalski1979]] [[campbell1959]].

In her study of the genres of Paradise Lost Lewalski also treated the hexaemeral poem as one of the forms Milton absorbed, and Du Bartas as the most influential modern example. Scholars debate whether the Weeks should be called an epic at all: the First Week is didactic and encyclopaedic rather than narrative, while the Second moves towards biblical epic, and its incompleteness left the form open for later poets [[lewalski1985]] [[prescott1978]].

debates.title: Du Bartas and Milton
text: That Milton read Sylvester's Du Bartas in his youth has long been assumed; Charles Dunster argued for it in 1800, and George Coffin Taylor's Milton's Use of Du Bartas (1934) assembled hundreds of parallels to argue that Paradise Lost owes far more to the Weeks than to any other modern poem. The parallels include the brooding Spirit, the description of the creatures, the Muse Urania, the fortunate fall and many turns of phrase [[taylor1934]].

Later scholars have been more cautious. Arnold Williams and J. M. Evans showed that much of the shared material belongs to the common tradition of commentary on Genesis, which both poets drew on independently, and Grant McColley placed Milton among a wide range of sources. The present consensus is that Milton knew the Weeks well and sometimes echoes them, but that direct borrowing is harder to prove than Taylor thought, and that the differences, above all in the treatment of Satan and of Adam's choice, matter more than the likenesses [[williams1948]] [[evans1968]] [[mccolley1940]] [[fowler1998]].

debates.title: Science and wonder
text: The Weeks are a major document of sixteenth-century 'scientific poetry', the French tradition studied by Albert-Marie Schmidt, in which poets versified cosmology, natural history and medicine. Du Bartas draws on Aristotle, Pliny and modern encyclopaedias, and does not separate observation from legend; the purpose of knowledge is wonder at the Creator [[schmidt1938]].

Modern readers often single out his rejection of Copernicus in the Fourth Day. In context it is the ordinary learned opinion of the 1570s, presented with real knowledge of the hypothesis; what is distinctive is the poem's role in making the Ptolemaic universe vivid for a vast readership, at the moment when that universe was about to be overturned. The French commentaries printed with the Sepmaine show how seriously its science was taken [[holmes1935]] [[dauphine1983]].

debates.title: Translation and amplification
text: Sylvester's version is considerably longer than the French. He expands phrases, adds compound epithets and inserts whole passages of English matter: rivers and places in Kent and Berkshire, tributes to Sidney, Spenser and Daniel, praise of Elizabeth and James, the Armada, Essex at Cadiz, the Gunpowder Plot and the plague. Susan Snyder's edition, which marks these additions, made it possible to see the translation as a distinct English poem [[snyder1979]].

Scholars disagree on how to judge this. Earlier critics such as Ashton saw Sylvester as a diffuse and sometimes clumsy amplifier; more recent work by Anne Lake Prescott and Peter Auger treats him as an adapter who naturalised a foreign Protestant poem, made it a book of the Jacobean court, and shaped the way English and Scottish readers received Du Bartas [[ashton1908]] [[prescott1978]] [[auger2019]].

debates.title: Reputation's rise and fall
text: In the generation after 1605 Sylvester's Du Bartas was one of the most admired books in English; its ingenious epithets were imitated and it was quoted in sermons and commonplace books. By the Restoration taste had changed. In the dedication of The Spanish Friar (1681) Dryden recalled that as a boy he had thought Sylvester superior to Spenser, and quoted the winter lines from 'The Handi-Crafts' as an example of the bombast that had once dazzled him [[ker1900]].

The poem never recovered its English popularity, and in France too Du Bartas was neglected after the classical age, though Goethe defended him. Modern scholarship has restored him as a major Renaissance poet, but debate continues over whether his style, so admired in its time, can be enjoyed today or only understood historically [[pellissier1883]] [[dauphine1983]] [[pouey2021]].

debates.title: Bradstreet and the colonial reception
text: Anne Bradstreet's poems, published in London as The Tenth Muse (1650), include an elegy 'In Honour of Du Bartas' and a set of long didactic poems on the four elements, humours, ages and seasons whose method and manner owe much to the Weeks; her 'Four Monarchies' draws chiefly on Ralegh's History of the World but continues the same tradition of versified sacred and universal history [[hensley1967]].

Her case shows that Du Bartas's influence crossed the Atlantic with the Puritan settlers, for whom a learned, encyclopaedic and strictly Protestant poem was an ideal model. Critics have debated whether her early poems are mere imitation or a deliberate apprenticeship to the most respectable model available to a woman poet [[auger2019]].

debates.title: The royal connection
text: James VI's translation of L'Uranie (1584), Du Bartas's visit to Scotland in 1587 and his French version of James's Lepanto created an exchange between a French Protestant poet and a Scottish king who wished to be known as a poet. The praise of James in the Second Week belongs to this relationship [[craigie1955]].

When James became king of England in 1603, the connection gave the English translation a court setting: Sylvester dedicated the Weeks to him and filled them with compliments to the Stuarts. Peter Auger's study of Du Bartas in England and Scotland reads the reception as a story of literary politics as much as of taste [[auger2019]].

quotes.quote:
THou, glorious Guide of Heav'ns star-glistring motion,
Thou, thou (true Neptune) Tamer of the Ocean,
quotes.explanation: The opening invocation addresses God with the titles of pagan deities (Neptune), corrected by the word 'true'. Christian poetry takes over the forms of classical poetry and claims their truth for itself. The compound 'star-glistring' is typical of Sylvester's diction.

quotes.quote:
The World's a Book in Folio, printed all
With God's great Works in letters Capitall:
Each Creature is a Page; and each Effect,
Afaire Character, void of all defect.
quotes.explanation: The governing image of the First Week: the creation as a printed book, legible to all. The image of a folio is apt for a poem that was itself issued as a great folio. (The run-together 'Afaire' is the edition's.)

quotes.quote:
That first World (yet) was a most formless Form,
A confus'd Heap, a Chaos most deform,
A Gulf of Gulfs, a Body ill compact,
An vgly medly, where all difference lackt:
quotes.explanation: Chaos is defined by paradox ('formless Form') and by the absence of difference: creation, in the poem's account, is the making of distinctions. Compare Milton's 'vast immeasurable Abyss' in Paradise Lost 7.

quotes.quote:
Therefore, for my part, I haue vow'd to Heav'n
Such wit and learning as my God hath giv'n;
To write, to th' honour of my Maker dread,
Verse that a Virgine without blush may read.
quotes.explanation: The vow of chaste and sacred verse, which made Du Bartas the model of the Christian poet for Protestant England. It answers the erotic poetry the poet has just condemned.

quotes.quote:
Arm'd with these reasons, 'twere superfluous
T' assail the reasons of Copernicus;
Who, to salve better, of the Stars th' appearance,
Vnto the Earth a three-fold motion warrants:
quotes.explanation: The poem's dismissal of heliocentrism, after physical arguments against the earth's motion. It shows both the poet's knowledge of the new astronomy and his confidence in the traditional cosmos.

quotes.quote:
Ther is no Theam more plentifull to sean,
Then is the glorious goodly Frame of MAN:
For in Man's self is Fire, Aire, Earth, and Sea;
Man's (in a word) the World's Epitomé
quotes.explanation: Man as the microcosm or 'little world', containing all the elements of the great one. The Sixth Day then anatomises him as thoroughly as the poem has described the universe.

quotes.quote:
THe cunning Painter, that with curious care,
Limning a Land-scape, various, rich, and rare,
quotes.explanation: The opening of the famous simile of God as a painter admiring his finished work, which turns the Sabbath rest into contemplation and justifies the poem's own delight in detail.

quotes.quote:
Cunningly adding her quaint smiling glances,
Her witty speech, and pretty countenances,
She so preuails, that her blind Lord at last,
A morsell of the sharp-sweet fruit doth taste.
quotes.who: The poet, of Eve and Adam
quotes.explanation: Adam's fall is told in four lines, as a seduction by Eve's charm. The brevity and the absence of any choice by Adam are a useful contrast with Paradise Lost 9, where Adam falls 'not deceav'd' but out of love.

quotes.quote:
But, when the Winters keener breath began
To crystallize the Baltike Ocean,
To glaze the Lakes, and bridle-vp the Floods,
And perriwig with wooll the bald-pate Woods;
quotes.explanation: The lines Dryden quoted as the 'fustian' he had admired in boyhood. They show the wit of Sylvester's metaphors (snow as a wig on the bald winter trees) and why later taste found them grotesque.

quotes.quote:
Vouch safe mee yet his Verse, and (Lord) I craue
Let me his Harp-strings, not his Bowe-strings haue;
quotes.explanation: The poet asks to inherit David's poetry rather than his military glory. David, the royal psalmist, is the poem's ideal of the sacred poet, and a model for James VI.

questions.q: Why does Du Bartas give so much space to natural history in a poem about the Creation?
questions.hint: Think about the 'book of nature', the hexaemeral tradition of Basil and Ambrose, and the moral lessons of the Seventh Day.

questions.q: How does the poem present the relation between sacred and profane poetry?
questions.hint: Consider the opening of the Second Day, L'Uranie, the call to Spenser and Daniel in 'Eden', and the praise of David's harp.

questions.q: What does the painter simile at the start of the Seventh Day suggest about God, the world and the poem itself?
questions.hint: Compare the detail of the painting with the catalogues of the previous Days.

questions.q: Compare the temptation and fall in 'The Imposture' with Paradise Lost 9. What does each poet emphasise?
questions.hint: Look at Satan's role, the serpent's speeches, Eve's hesitation and Adam's silence or choice.

questions.q: How does Du Bartas deal with the scientific controversies of his time, such as the motion of the earth or the matter of the heavens?
questions.hint: Read the Copernicus passage in the Fourth Day and the discussion of the heavens at the end of the Second Day.

questions.q: In what ways is Sylvester's version an English poem rather than simply a translation?
questions.hint: Find the passages about Kent and Berkshire, Sidney, Elizabeth, James, Cadiz and the Gunpowder Plot.

questions.q: What view of kingship emerges from the Second Week?
questions.hint: Consider Nimrod, the debate in 'The Captaines', David's counsel to Solomon, and the elders' advice to Rehoboam.

questions.q: Why might the Weeks have been so popular in early seventeenth-century England, and why did they lose favour?
questions.hint: Think about Protestant taste, the royal connection, the encyclopaedic method, and Dryden's judgement in 1681.

questions.q: How does the Second Week use typology to connect Old Testament history with Christ?
questions.hint: Look at Isaac, the Passover, the manna and the closing prayer for the heavenly Jerusalem.

questions.q: What is the role of allegorical figures (the Furies, Envy, Sleep, Nature) in a poem that insists on the literal truth of Scripture?
questions.hint: Ask whether they explain, dramatise or decorate the biblical narrative.
